summary: Compares IPv6 transition technologies that provide IPv4-as-a-Service for ISPs running IPv6-only access or core networks. It examines the main technologies and their advantages and disadvantages, to help an operator choose based on topology, skills, and strategy. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some networks only speak the new address language but customers still need the old one. This weighs different translators, like choosing a tool for a job.

questions: which ipv4-as-a-service technology should i use
what are the pros and cons of 464xlat and dslite
what is ipv4 as a service
how many ports does a nat subscriber need
what is the difference between map-e and map-t
subtitle: A buyer's guide to the five main ways an IPv6-only ISP can keep serving IPv4 to its customers.

tldr.problem: ISPs that run IPv6-only access or core networks still have to give customers IPv4 service, and the IETF has standardized several different ways to do it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares five IPv4-as-a-Service technologies (464XLAT, Dual-Stack Lite, lightweight 4over6, MAP-E and MAP-T) by how they cross the IPv6 network, where they keep state, how they share addresses, and what they cost to run.
tldr.outcome: There is no single winner. The best choice depends on the operator's topology, skills, strategy and other preferences, and the RFC lays out the trade-offs to help decide.

today: RFC 9313 is an Informational RFC from October 2022. Its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFCs, and the RFC itself notes that its performance and security comparisons were still planned work.

sections.title: Why a Comparison Is Needed
sections.content:
Network operators are moving toward single-stack IPv6 core and access networks to simplify planning and operations. Customers, however, still need IPv4 for the foreseeable future. IPv4-as-a-Service (IPv4aaS) is the family of technologies that delivers it over an IPv6-only network.

The IETF has standardized several of these, and picking among them is time-consuming. This informational RFC compares the five most commonly used: 464XLAT (RFC 6877), Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333), Lightweight 4over6 (RFC 7596), MAP-E (RFC 7597) and MAP-T (RFC 7599). It is a reference for choosing, not a protocol specification.
sections.eli5: There are five ways to let old-style internet traffic ride on a new-style network. This guide helps an internet company pick the one that fits.

sections.title: The Five Technologies at a Glance
sections.content:
464XLAT uses a customer-side translator (CLAT) that statelessly turns IPv4 into IPv6, and a provider-side translator (PLAT) that does stateful NAT64 into the IPv4 Internet. It is typically combined with DNS64, so IPv6-only clients need only a single translation, and the CLAT is used just for traffic from IPv4-only applications or literal IPv4 addresses.

Dual-Stack Lite has the customer router (the B4) wrap IPv4 packets inside IPv6 and send them to an AFTR, which unwraps them and performs stateful NAPT44. Lightweight 4over6 is a variant that moves the stateful NAPT44 from the central AFTR into the customer's device, so the lwAFTR only keeps a binding table and does encapsulation.

MAP-E and MAP-T use a stateless algorithm that embeds part of the customer's IPv4 address and port range into the delegated IPv6 prefix, so one MAP rule can cover many clients. MAP-E encapsulates IPv4 in IPv6; MAP-T uses double stateless translation (NAT46 in the CE and NAT64 in the border router).
sections.eli5: Some of these put the old-style message inside a new-style envelope. Others rewrite the address on the message itself. They also differ in who does the bookkeeping: the customer's box or the company's big box.

sections.title: Crossing the Network and Sharing Addresses
sections.content:
There are two ways to cross the IPv6 provider network: 4-6-4 translation (464XLAT, MAP-T) or 4in6 encapsulation (DS-Lite, lw4o6, MAP-E). Both make packets bigger than native IPv4. Translation adds 20 bytes (the 20-byte IPv4 header becomes a 40-byte IPv6 header), while encapsulation adds 40 bytes. The RFC advises managing the MTU in the IPv6-only domain so that no fragmentation happens inside it.

Translation yields native IPv6 packets with a transport-layer header, which helps ECMP hashing and ACL filtering, but it cannot translate IPv4 header options or multicast and, with address sharing, carries only port-aware protocols such as TCP and UDP plus ICMP. Encapsulation carries any IP protocol intact.

Address sharing needs a stateful NAPT somewhere. The CGN-based approaches (DS-Lite, 464XLAT) keep per-session state for all active clients in the operator network. The A+P approaches (lw4o6, MAP-E, MAP-T) keep it in the customer's CE and only for devices in the home, leaving the central element stateless.
sections.eli5: Both tricks make each message a bit heavier, so the road must be wide enough. Either a central helper keeps track of everyone's conversations, or each home keeps track of its own.

sections.title: Port Budgets and Address Pool Size
sections.content:
Sharing one public IPv4 address means sharing its ports. The RFC cites a study that a device behind a NAT could use up to 300 ports at once, and estimates a residential subscriber at about 1,200 ports when four port-hungry applications talk to the same destination. If 80% of traffic goes to IPv6 destinations, only 20% needs IPv4 ports, so 240 ports per subscriber. With 64,511 usable ports per address, a /22 would serve over 275,000 subscribers.

That conservative figure fits 464XLAT because its NAT64 allocates ports dynamically. The other technologies often need a fixed, pre-provisioned port range, so a typical figure of 2,000 ports gives 30 subscribers per address, and a /19 would serve 245,760 subscribers.

Too few ports causes hard-to-debug failures, so the RFC recommends a conservatively large fixed allocation. Too many wastes scarce IPv4 addresses. Changing port ranges in A+P schemes needs more planning, although lw4o6 can reprovision a single customer through its per-customer binding table entry.
sections.eli5: An address is like one phone line shared by many people, and ports are the extensions. Give each person too few extensions and calls fail. Give too many and you run out of lines.

sections.title: Servers, Logging, Load Sharing and Deployment
sections.content:
Customers who want to run a public server need a way to get a public port. With stateful operator-side NAT, that means the Port Control Protocol (PCP), which the RFC says is required for server operation with 464XLAT. With A+P schemes the user can serve on an allocated port, though operators commonly do not assign well-known ports unless a full IPv4 address is given.

Logging differs sharply. Stateful 464XLAT and DS-Lite must log every session to meet data-retention laws, which is a heavy burden. Allocating a block of ports per client cuts the logging but shares addresses less efficiently. Stateless schemes only need to keep their MAP rules or binding table with timestamps, but cannot provide per-session logs if a law demands them.

For load sharing, stateless schemes can use anycast, and flows may take asymmetric paths. Stateful CGNs need ECMP plus state synchronization between nodes to survive failures and asymmetric routing.

On deployment, several cellular networks use 464XLAT and no other of the five. In broadband, DS-Lite is the most common, with lw4o6 growing quickly. Reported 464XLAT traffic data show about 75% of cellular traffic is IPv6 end to end, 24% needs one translation and under 1% needs two. OpenWRT code sizes were 17 kB, 35 kB, 15 kB, 35 kB and 48 kB for 464XLAT, lw4o6, DS-Lite, MAP-E and MAP-T.
sections.eli5: Some systems have to write down every single call for the police, which is a lot of paper. Others just keep one short rule book. Which is easier depends on what the law asks for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Logs may contain personally identifiable information, so care is needed when storing, sending and giving access to them. This applies to logging in general, not only to IPv4aaS.

Restricting a subscriber to a small port set lowers the entropy of source ports, for example from 16 bits to 10 bits with 1024 ports each, which makes DNS cache poisoning theoretically easier for lw4o6, MAP-E and MAP-T. The RFC considers the chance of successful exploitation low, because the attack needs the subscriber to run their own caching DNS server and the attacker to be inside the provider network. Encapsulation-based technologies have no DNSSEC implications, while translation-based ones may. Implementers should also consult the security sections of the RFCs for each technology.
sections.eli5: If a house only has a few mailbox numbers, a trickster has fewer guesses to make. The paper says this is a small risk, but it is worth knowing.
